claims.text: A machine-learning model integrating high-dimensional alloy-composition and microstructural-disorder representations can predict low phonon thermal conductivity in high-entropy alloys more accurately than conventional empirical models.
Lattice distortions and mass-fluctuation scattering are relevant descriptors for predicting phonon thermal conductivity in high-entropy alloys.
The target materials have high configurational entropy and a predominantly homogeneous phase distribution.
The predictive framework uses detailed compositional and microstructural descriptors as input features.
The model is applicable to single-phase, homogeneous high-entropy alloys with configurational entropy greater than approximately 1.5R.
The model has limited applicability to alloys with significant phase separation or uncharacterized nanostructural features.
High-dimensional compositional and microstructural descriptors can implicitly capture lattice disorder and mass-fluctuation scattering.
Local compositional fluctuations and microstructural disorder influence phonon-scattering events.
Phonon-scattering events caused by compositional fluctuations and microstructural disorder reduce heat conduction.
Correlating high-dimensional descriptors with phonon-scattering behavior enables better predictions than lower-dimensional regression or physical models.
The proposed model will reduce mean absolute prediction error by approximately 20% or more relative to conventional empirical methods.
Rule-of-mixtures, simple regression, and Debye–Callaway-type models constitute the baseline conventional approaches.
Secondary phases can significantly alter thermal-transport dynamics and therefore restrict the model's applicability to multiphase alloys.
Inaccurate characterization of microstructural features may reduce the model's robustness.
Laser-flash analysis can be used as part of determining experimental phonon thermal conductivity for the benchmark.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant mean-absolute-error reduction of approximately 20% relative to conventional baselines would falsify the proposed performance hypothesis.
